title: 1 Samuel 26:1–12
context: As in chapter 23, the Ziphites report David’s hiding place to Saul, who comes with three thousand chosen men to the wilderness of Ziph. David scouts the camp and goes down by night with Abishai into the place where Saul lies sleeping among his troops. Abishai urges him to strike Saul with his own spear, but David refuses to stretch out his hand against the LORD’s anointed, trusting that the LORD will deal with Saul in his own time. He takes the spear and the water jar instead, and no one wakes, because a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen on them. Like the sparing at En Gedi in chapter 24, readers in both traditions commonly treat this as shared ground about restraint, trust in God’s timing, and respect for God-given office.

verses.text: The Ziphites came to Saul to Gibeah, saying, “Doesn’t David hide himself in the hill of Hachilah, which is before the desert?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the Ziphites again report David’s hiding place to Saul, as they did earlier (compare 1 Samuel 23:19). Betrayal recurs.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repetition as part of the narrative pattern that tests David’s faith. Readers in both traditions commonly hold the location of the hill of Hachilah with caution.

verses.text: Then Saul arose and went down to the wilderness of Ziph, having three thousand chosen men of Israel with him, to seek David in the wilderness of Ziph.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Saul going down with three thousand chosen men to seek David. Despite his earlier confession in chapter 24, he pursues David again.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Saul’s renewed pursuit as showing that his earlier words did not reflect lasting change. Both traditions commonly read the verse as revealing the instability of Saul’s heart.

verses.text: Saul encamped in the hill of Hachilah, which is before the desert, by the way. But David stayed in the wilderness, and he saw that Saul came after him into the wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Saul encamping by the way while David stays in the wilderness and watches. David remains alert to the danger.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David’s watchfulness as prudence under God’s care. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as setting the scene for the night visit.

verses.text: David therefore sent out spies, and understood that Saul had certainly come.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David sending spies to confirm Saul’s arrival. He acts with careful wisdom rather than reacting in fear or haste.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David using ordinary means while trusting God. Both traditions commonly read the verse as an example of wise action under threat.

verses.text: Then David arose and came to the place where Saul had encamped; and David saw the place where Saul lay, with Abner the son of Ner, the captain of his army. Saul lay within the place of the wagons, and the people were encamped around him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David approaching the camp and seeing Saul lying among the wagons with Abner nearby. David takes a bold risk.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the detailed description of Saul’s protected position as heightening the drama. Readers in both traditions commonly note that Saul appears secure, though the story will show otherwise.

verses.text: Then David answered and said to Ahimelech the Hittite, and to Abishai the son of Zeruiah, brother of Joab, saying, “Who will go down with me to Saul to the camp?” Abishai said, “I will go down with you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note David asking Ahimelech the Hittite and Abishai who will go with him, and Abishai volunteering. Courage is shown by a loyal companion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Abishai, brother of Joab, introduced as a bold and zealous warrior. Both traditions commonly read the verse as preparing for the contrast between Abishai’s zeal and David’s restraint.

verses.text: So David and Abishai came to the people by night; and, behold, Saul lay sleeping within the place of the wagons, with his spear stuck in the ground at his head; and Abner and the people lay around him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David and Abishai finding Saul asleep with his spear stuck in the ground at his head. The king is completely vulnerable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the scene as God placing Saul within David’s reach. Readers in both traditions commonly read the image of the spear as a symbol of Saul’s power, now at David’s disposal.

verses.text: Then Abishai said to David, “God has delivered up your enemy into your hand today. Now therefore please let me strike him with the spear to the earth at one stroke, and I will not strike him the second time.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Abishai interpreting the moment as God delivering Saul into David’s hand and offering to kill him with one stroke. Opportunity is mistaken for permission.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Abishai’s reasoning echoing the suggestion of David’s men in the cave (1 Samuel 24:4). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a temptation to take God’s purposes into one’s own hands.

verses.text: David said to Abishai, “Don’t destroy him, for who can stretch out his hand against the LORD’s anointed, and be guiltless?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David refusing to harm the LORD’s anointed, asking who could do so and be guiltless. He respects the office God established.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David’s refusal as reverence for God’s appointment, consistent with his earlier words (1 Samuel 24:6). Readers in both traditions commonly see this restraint as a mark of faith.

verses.text: David said, “As the LORD lives, the LORD will strike him; or his day shall come to die, or he shall go down into battle and perish.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David trusting that the LORD will deal with Saul, whether by striking him, by natural death, or in battle. He leaves the timing to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David’s confidence in God’s sovereign timing, later fulfilled when Saul dies in battle (1 Samuel 31:4). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a model of waiting on God (compare Psalm 37:7).

verses.text: The LORD forbid that I should stretch out my hand against the LORD’s anointed; but now please take the spear that is at his head and the jar of water, and let’s go.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David again refusing to stretch out his hand and taking only the spear and water jar. He chooses restraint over revenge.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the taking of the spear and jar as proof of his opportunity and his mercy. Readers in both traditions commonly see the verse as a deliberate act of integrity.

verses.text: So David took the spear and the jar of water from Saul’s head, and they went away. No man saw it, or knew it, nor did any awake; for they were all asleep, because a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen on them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that no one woke because a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen on them. God protects David as he acts with restraint.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s direct involvement in the deep sleep (compare Genesis 2:21; 15:12). Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing God working alongside David’s faithful choices.
